fr-bnp-paribas.conditions: BNP Paribas publishes a separate non-resident price for an active euro current account, so an existing account can continue after the holder stops residing in France, but at non-resident pricing. The holder must tell the bank about changes (the convention says the client must provide 'sans délai' any information, change or supporting document useful for the account, including a change of address) and complete a FATCA/CRS self-certification. The bank can close the account at any time with 2 months' notice (convention clause: 'La Banque peut, à tout moment, clôturer le compte ... la Banque accorde au Client un délai de préavis de 2 mois'), or without notice for seriously reprehensible behaviour. BNP Paribas has a dedicated 'filière Non-Résidents' (international branches) for expatriates. Inactive accounts (L312-19 CMF) cost 30 EUR a year.
fr-bnp-paribas.nonResidentFee: Tenue de compte actif en euros for clients not resident in France: 10 EUR/month if resident in the EU or an EAI (CRS) country; 15 EUR/month if resident in a non-EAI country. The brochure's footnote (3) says: 'Les États-Unis ne font pas partie des pays EAI', so a US resident pays 15 EUR/month. Reduced by 2.50 EUR/month when an 'Esprit Libre' package fee is charged. The same page lists 'Tenue de compte pour les clients âgés de moins de 25 ans: Gratuit', but does not say whether that also waives the non-resident fee.
fr-bnp-paribas.usResidentPolicy: The bank publishes no refusal or closure policy for US persons. The convention says FATCA and the OCDE CRS standard require the bank to identify its clients' tax residences and 'plus spécifiquement d'identifier les US Person', collecting a self-certification and supporting documents. The bank is also a US Qualified Intermediary (QI). In the 2019-2021 'Américains accidentels' episode, the press and a 2021 parliamentary question reported that at least one major French bank notified US-born clients that their accounts would be closed if no US TIN was provided. The bank was not named in official sources.

abroad.card: Card payment outside the euro zone: 2.90% + 0.90 EUR per transaction (Visa Infinite 2% + 0.60 EUR; virtual card no fee). Excludes FX, and conversion happens at the Visa network rate. Option Travel: 10 EUR/month for unlimited foreign-currency card payments and withdrawals with no per-transaction commission; free for clients aged 18-24.
abroad.atm: Withdrawal at another bank's ATM outside the euro zone: 2.90% + 3 EUR (Visa Infinite 2% + 2.20 EUR). No fee at BNP Paribas Global Network ATMs, Global Alliance ATMs, or with Option Travel. Global Alliance included Bank of America in the US according to BNP Paribas group press releases from 2001-2002. That was seen as search snippets and the current member list was not verified.
abroad.outgoing: Non-SEPA occasional transfer made online (Mes Comptes / mabanque): free when sent in the currency of the beneficiary's country (USD to a US account) if the required information is given, otherwise 15 EUR. When sent in EUR or another currency: 15 EUR (3 EUR to a BNP Paribas subsidiary). By branch or service client: 20 EUR (8 EUR to a subsidiary). Extras: 12.90 EUR if BIC/IBAN is missing or wrong, 20.50 EUR for OUR (no fees for the beneficiary), 7 EUR for urgent. Correspondent-bank fees may be deducted from the amount.
abroad.incoming: Receipt of a non-SEPA transfer: 11 EUR per transfer.
abroad.fxMargin: Exchange rate 'en vigueur au moment de l'opération'. The brochure says it 'inclut la marge commerciale de BNP Paribas', without quantifying the margin. Spot FX operations (outside transfer fees): 0.50 per mille, minimum 18 EUR.
abroad.days: Value date for non-SEPA transfers is the execution date (outgoing) or settlement date (incoming). No end-to-end delivery time is published for transfers to the US.
abroad.opening: BNP Paribas says it runs a dedicated 'filière Non-Résidents' (created 2018: a network of about 27-30 branches, including specialist international branches in Paris, a private-banking centre and a remote support team) for expatriates and foreign clients, and that account opening is possible 'depuis la France ou de l'étranger'. That comes from search snippets of mabanque.bnpparibas and group.bnpparibas pages, which returned HTTP 403 when fetched. No published remote-opening eligibility list or country exclusions were found.
abroad.kyc: At opening, the bank checks identity and address. Under FATCA and CRS it collects a tax-residence self-certification and supporting documents to establish tax status and identify US Persons. As a US Qualified Intermediary it may ask for specific US documents. The client must provide 'sans délai' any change and supporting documents, including a change of contact details. The bank-specific documents were not published: W-9 for a US person, W-8BEN otherwise, and the form for a change of tax residence. The general French practice is a new self-certification when circumstances change (see the country notes).
abroad.taxAtSource: France: interest paid to a person whose tax household is outside France is exempt from French tax (CGI art. 125 A III) unless the person lives in a non-cooperative state or territory (ETNC), where a 75% levy applies. No CSG/CRDS is due for non-residents (impots.gouv.fr). BNP's brochure publishes no bank-specific rule.

assumptions: SLATE assumes the 15 EUR/month non-EAI non-resident fee applies to a US-resident student, because BNP's brochure states the US is not an EAI country.

SLATE assumes the under-25 'tenue de compte gratuit' line does not waive the non-resident fee, because the brochure does not say it does. A student under 25 might in practice pay nothing, so treat this as uncertain.

SLATE assumes the 2019 Banque Privée convention's 2-month bank-closure clause matches the current retail convention, since that is the statutory minimum under CMF L312-1-1. The current mabanque convention could not be fetched (HTTP 403).
SLATE assumes online and app access keeps working from the US with a US mobile number registered for Clé Digitale. Nothing published was found confirming or excluding foreign numbers.
SLATE assumes Bank of America ATMs are still in Global Alliance. This is based only on a 2002 press-release snippet.

fr-societe-generale.conditions: SG publishes a quarterly 'frais de gestion administrative pour les clients non-résidents', so accounts of non-residents continue at extra cost. The client must tell SG 'dès que celui-ci survient' of any change of tax-residence country, from French tax resident to non-resident, and of acquiring US citizenship or a green card. SG then collects a new self-certification. Before a permanent move abroad, SG asks the client to contact their adviser to update postal address and phone. SG may close the account on its own initiative by registered letter 'moyennant le respect d'un délai de préavis de 2 mois, sans avoir à en indiquer le motif'. It may close on the same terms if the client refuses to provide documents required for its legal or regulatory obligations, and with no notice for seriously reprehensible behaviour or abnormal account operation (CG art. 'Clôture à l'initiative de la Banque').
fr-societe-generale.nonResidentFee: Frais de gestion administrative pour les clients non-résidents (capped at one charge per client per quarter, on top of account-keeping fees): EU residents 25 EUR/quarter; residents of an EAI country 50 EUR/quarter; residents of a non-EAI country 75 EUR/quarter. Exempt: clients under 25, Banque Privée clients, inactive accounts, Généris holders, Services Bancaires de Base holders. The standard account-keeping fee is 7.65 EUR/quarter, exempt under 25 and with JAZZ/Sobrio etc. A footnote reads '(1) Exonération pour les non-résidents', but the item it attaches to is unclear in the extracted text. SG does not say whether the US counts as EAI.
fr-societe-generale.usResidentPolicy: SG publishes no blanket refusal or closure of US persons. The CG say SG must identify clients who are US taxpayers under FATCA or residents of CRS (NCD/EAI) countries and report them via the French tax administration to the IRS or the residence country. Under CMF L564-1, a bank that cannot identify a holder's tax residences and TINs 'n'établit pas de relation contractuelle'. Refusal to provide required documents is a stated ground for closure with 2 months' notice. The client must report acquiring US citizenship or a green card.

abroad.card: Payment in a currency other than EUR (other cards): 2.7% for payments of 10 EUR or less; 1.00 EUR + 2.7% for more than 10 EUR (CB Visa Infinite: 2% / 1 EUR + 2%). Conversion is at the Visa/Mastercard rate. Fees are waived with Option Internationale (from 11 EUR/month; 'Étudiants de moins de 30 ans' level 3 EUR/month, or 2 EUR with Sobrio/JAZZ) or Carte Collection Option Voyageur (28 EUR/year).
abroad.atm: ATM withdrawal in non-EUR currency (other cards): 3.00 EUR + 2.7% (Visa Infinite 3.00 EUR + 2%). The ATM operator may add its own fee. Waived under Option Internationale levels and Option Voyageur.
abroad.outgoing: Non-SEPA occasional transfer from the Espace Client or L'Appli SG, SHARE option: 9.00 EUR up to 500 EUR, 13.00 EUR above 500 EUR. OUR option adds 23.00 EUR. Through an SG agent: 13.00 EUR up to 500 EUR, otherwise 0.10% (min 26 EUR, max 70 EUR), plus 23 EUR for OUR. Correspondent or beneficiary bank fees may be added. SG automatically converts USD-denominated orders sent to beneficiaries outside the US.
abroad.incoming: Receipt of a non-SEPA transfer: free up to 150 EUR; 22.00 EUR per transfer above 150 EUR.
abroad.fxMargin: The rate is the SG trading-room price at execution plus a commercial margin, which 'dépend du montant de la transaction et de la devise concernée'. Published example: on 06/10/2025 the EUR/USD rate of 1.1678 became 1.1515 after margin for buying 1,000 USD (about 1.4%). Card transactions use the Visa/Mastercard rate.
abroad.days: Not published for non-SEPA transfers in the brochure.
abroad.opening: Not published as a remote non-resident opening product. The CG require a tax-residence self-certification from any applicant 'quel que soit le pays de résidence fiscale'. SG's documents quote the statutory droit au compte: any French national resident outside France who has no deposit account in France can get one via the Banque de France designation procedure. No SG-specific remote opening channel for non-residents was found.
abroad.kyc: At opening: ID, proof of address, and the bank's tax-residence self-certification form, plus any document needed to establish tax status. During the relationship, the client must report in writing, without delay, any change: civil status, nationality, home, tax or postal address, acquisition of US citizenship or a green card, transfer of tax residence to another state, phone or email. SG then collects a new self-certification. SG is not liable for applying the original tax regime if not informed. W-9 and W-8BEN are not named in the CG.
abroad.taxAtSource: France: interest paid to a non-resident is exempt from French tax (CGI art. 125 A III) unless the person lives in an ETNC, where a 75% levy applies. No CSG/CRDS for non-residents (impots.gouv.fr). The SG CG add that a non-resident client must check the tax rules of their country of residence.

assumptions: SLATE assumes SG treats the US as a non-EAI country (75 EUR/quarter), since the US is not a CRS participant. BNP's brochure says so explicitly but SG's does not, and LCL treats the US as EAI (which would mean 50 EUR/quarter).
SLATE assumes the under-25 exemption means a student aged 24 or under pays no non-resident administrative fee.
SLATE assumes transfer delivery time to the US is 1-3 business days, since SG does not publish it.
SLATE assumes SG would ask a US-person client for a W-9 and others for a W-8BEN. The CG name only the tax-residence self-certification.

fr-lcl.conditions: LCL prices accounts of clients resident outside France, so they can be kept. The fee depends on residence and on whether the client 'domicilie ses revenus chez LCL' (has income paid in). Online-banking access is suspended if mail comes back 'NPAI'/'PND' until the new address is given and proven, so the address must be kept up to date. A FATCA/EAI self-certification is mandatory. LCL's account convention was not retrieved. Bank-initiated closure therefore falls under the statutory minimum of 2 months' notice (CMF L312-1-1).
fr-lcl.nonResidentFee: Tenue de compte, client résidant hors de l'Union Européenne (per account per quarter): free for a deposit or Compte Sur Livret account of a resident of an EAI country who has income paid in at LCL; 40.00 EUR/quarter for an EAI-country resident who does not; 80.00 EUR/quarter for residents of other countries. LCL's footnote says 'les États-Unis et le Maroc sont également considérés comme des pays EAI', so a US resident pays 0 or 40 EUR/quarter. Exempt: clients under 26, LCL Initial subscribers, droit au compte accounts and inactive accounts. For comparison, French residents pay 10 EUR/quarter if no income is paid in.
fr-lcl.usResidentPolicy: LCL publishes that 'toute personne née aux États-Unis est un citoyen américain et donc un contribuable américain'. US citizens or tax residents must provide a W-9 (US taxpayers) and the self-certification (the page lists W-8BEN for individuals). 'LCL n'est pas autorisé à entrer en relation ou à ouvrir de nouveaux comptes à des clients refusant de fournir les attestations requises.' For existing clients with discrepancies, LCL asks them to resubmit forms (declaration.fatca@lcl.fr). No published closure of US persons who comply.

abroad.card: Card payment in a foreign currency or outside the EEA: 1.26 EUR + 3.05% per payment (Mastercard Platinum+: 1.26 EUR + 2.38%). The percentage has a minimum of 0.80 EUR. Conversion is at the Visa/Mastercard rate.
abroad.atm: ATM withdrawal in a foreign currency or outside the EEA: 3.17 EUR + 3.05% (Mastercard Platinum+: 2.46 EUR + 2.38%). Over the counter: 5.59 EUR + 3.35% (Infinite/Platinum+: 4.06 EUR + 2.38%).
abroad.outgoing: Émission d'un virement non SEPA (euros outside SEPA, or any currency): fixed commission 26.70 EUR up to 80,000 EUR; 0.13% above 80,000 EUR. Reprocessing for incomplete or wrong information: 13.30 EUR. Recall request: 10.00 EUR. Plus a currency-conversion commission when there is conversion (see fxMargin).
abroad.incoming: Réception d'un virement non SEPA: flat commission 20.00 EUR.
abroad.fxMargin: Where there is currency conversion, a proportional change commission of 0.05% up to 80,000 EUR and 0.025% above (minimum 20.00 EUR) is due. 'Le cours de change appliqué est celui de la devise scripturale chez LCL.' The margin built into that rate is not published.
abroad.days: Not published.
abroad.opening: Not published as a remote non-resident product. LCL's tariff explicitly prices accounts of residents outside the EU, so non-resident accounts exist. Any opening requires the FATCA/EAI self-certification, without which LCL will not open the account.
abroad.kyc: A FATCA and EAI self-certification is obligatory for every account opening (since 2016-01-01, CGI art. 1649 AC). US citizens or residents provide a W-9; the LCL page also lists the W-8BEN. LCL will not open accounts for clients who refuse the required attestations. Existing clients with inconsistencies are asked to resubmit forms by email or post to LCL's tax service. Proof of address can be demanded when security codes are posted. The account is blocked online after returned mail until a proven new address is supplied.
abroad.taxAtSource: France: interest paid to a non-resident is exempt from French tax (CGI art. 125 A III) unless the person lives in an ETNC, where a 75% levy applies. No CSG/CRDS for non-residents (impots.gouv.fr). LCL publishes no bank-specific rule.

assumptions: SLATE assumes LCL's bank-initiated closure notice is 2 months, the statutory minimum in CMF L312-1-1. LCL's account convention itself was not found.
SLATE assumes a student with no income paid into LCL pays 40 EUR/quarter, and pays nothing if under 26.
SLATE assumes foreign-currency (USD) transfers have to be ordered through the branch, because the online CG describe online transfers outside SEPA as euro transfers.
SLATE assumes the 2026-01-01 tariff remained in force through 2026-10-16. A later 2026 LCL tariff (moneyvox 'tarifs-2026-c') exists and was not read.

fr-credit-agricole.conditions: Crédit Agricole d'Île-de-France (CADIF) publishes no non-resident account fee and no rule closing accounts on departure, so the account continues on the convention's terms. The Crédit Agricole convention template requires a tax-residence self-certification, which may be asked for again after opening 'en cas de changement de circonstances'. The template allows the bank to end the convention 'à tout moment en respectant un préavis de deux mois', or immediately for serious anomalies. That convention is the national CGL_CPT_FUSIONNE text, read from the copy published by Crédit Agricole de La Réunion. The CADIF-specific convention was not found.
fr-credit-agricole.nonResidentFee: not published. CADIF's 2026 tariff has no non-resident line. The standard 'Frais de tenue de compte de dépôt' is 1.50 EUR/month.
fr-credit-agricole.usResidentPolicy: Crédit Agricole publishes that it must know whether a client is 'citoyen ou résident américain au sens de la législation FATCA (US Person)'. Before opening, the client must give their US TIN. The bank reports identity, balances and interest to the French tax administration for the IRS, and must report a client to the IRS if US indicia are found and not rebutted. The FATCA page adds that each US Person must obtain a TIN and give it to financial institutions. No published blanket refusal or closure of US persons. Third-party sites claim CA accepts Americans 'case by case', which is not official.

abroad.card: Card payments in the EEA in a non-euro currency and outside the EEA: 2.50% per operation for standard cards. Free with World Elite Mastercard or Visa Infinite, and free with Mastercard Mozaïc (debit) or the 18-30 Globe Trotter card. Conversion at the Visa/Mastercard rate, expressed as a margin over the ECB rate.
abroad.atm: Withdrawal outside euros (other cards): 3 EUR per withdrawal at an ATM; 2% + 6.70 EUR over the counter. Free with World Elite or Infinite cards. The Eko offer (addendum, 12/10/2026) charges 1 EUR per withdrawal outside the EEA in foreign currency with its optional physical card. Values come from an OCR-scanned PDF and the column pairing should be checked.
abroad.outgoing: International transfer sent (including UK and Switzerland), online ('Virement SELF CARE': no SWIFT fee), SHARE: 15 EUR minimum up to 15,000 EUR, 0.10% above (as printed; OCR text). OUR adds a 21.50 EUR surcharge. In branch: minimum 23 EUR up to 23,000 EUR, 0.10% above. Foreign bank fees may be added.
abroad.incoming: International transfer received (in foreign currency from any origin, or in euros from outside the EEA): 21.84 EUR. A footnote reduces this to 20% of the amount received for transfers under 107.60 EUR.
abroad.fxMargin: When CADIF performs the FX for a transfer, the rate is 'un cours unique sur la journée (cours d'achat ou cours de vente selon le sens) incluant une marge'. The client only learns it the next day. The margin is not quantified. Cheque FX negotiations carry a 0.05% change commission (min 20 EUR).
abroad.days: Not published for international transfers, beyond the 'cours unique sur la journée' known the next day.
abroad.opening: not published by CADIF. The convention template says the bank cannot open a product without a completed and signed self-certification. French nationals residing abroad have the statutory droit au compte (CMF L312-1).
abroad.kyc: Before opening, the client must state whether they are a US citizen or resident and if so give their US TIN, plus their tax-residence country or countries and tax ID numbers, all in the self-certification. The bank may ask again after opening, for example on a change of circumstances. If the file suggests a different residence than the one declared, the client must give a new self-certification or a reasonable explanation. Forms by name (W-9 / W-8BEN) are not published.
abroad.taxAtSource: France: interest paid to a non-resident is exempt from French tax (CGI art. 125 A III) unless the person lives in an ETNC, where a 75% levy applies. No CSG/CRDS for non-residents (impots.gouv.fr).

assumptions: SLATE assumes CADIF charges no non-resident surcharge, because none is published, so a student abroad pays the standard 1.50 EUR/month account fee.
SLATE assumes CADIF's own convention carries the same 2-month bank-closure clause as the national Crédit Agricole template (read from the La Réunion copy), which is also the statutory minimum.
SLATE assumes the scanned tariff's figures are read correctly. They came from OCR of a scanned PDF (online international transfer 15 EUR minimum up to 15,000 EUR; ATM outside euro 3 EUR; card 2.50%).
SLATE assumes a student aged 18-30 gets one free CADIF outgoing international transfer per month under the published refund.

fr-la-banque-postale.conditions: La Banque Postale publishes no non-resident fee and no rule closing on departure. The client must tell the bank of any change in situation, 'notamment son changement de résidence fiscale', and give a new self-certification of tax residence(s) and TIN(s) when the country of tax residence changes. If the documents establishing tax residence and TIN are not provided, or appear incomplete or wrong, an existing account 'pourra être clôturé, à la seule initiative de la Banque'. The convention lets the bank end it by registered letter. The extracted wording does not show the notice. The statutory minimum for bank-initiated closure is 2 months (CMF L312-1-1). Accounts with no movement for 12 months can be closed by the bank with 60 days' notice. Immediate closure is possible for abnormal operation, fraud, refusal to meet an essential information duty, or false documents.
fr-la-banque-postale.nonResidentFee: not published. LBP's 2026 tariff has no non-resident line. Standard tenue de compte is 2.10 EUR/month, and accounts with no movement or inactive cost 30 EUR/year.
fr-la-banque-postale.usResidentPolicy: LBP publishes no US-person-specific refusal or closure policy. Its convention ties account opening to a self-certification of tax residence(s) and TIN(s), and allows closure if these are not provided or are wrong. No LBP-specific FATCA page was read.

abroad.card: Card payment abroad in a currency other than EUR: 2.30% of the amount (Visa Platinum / Infinite 1.15%), capped at 6.00 EUR per operation. Free with Option Internationale activated (12 EUR per activation). Free for holders of a Formule de Compte Jeune (ages 12-29). Plus the Visa FX rate.
abroad.atm: Withdrawal at another bank's ATM in a non-EUR currency: 3.30 EUR + 2.30% of the amount. 2.00 EUR per operation with Option Internationale or a Formule de Compte Jeune. Cash advance at another bank's counter in foreign currency: 6.00 EUR + 2.30%.
abroad.outgoing: Non-SEPA occasional transfer sent online: 0.10% of the amount, minimum 9.90 EUR, maximum 70.00 EUR. At a post office or through the CREC: 0.10%, minimum 15.50 EUR, maximum 70 EUR. Optional OUR (correspondent fees paid by sender): up to 18.00 EUR. Change commission: 10.00 EUR. The beneficiary's or correspondent bank may charge extra.
abroad.incoming: Réception d'un virement non SEPA: 13.50 EUR.
abroad.fxMargin: Change commission of 10.00 EUR per transfer. The FX margin is not published. Card FX is at the Visa rate (for EEA currencies, ECB rate + X%).
abroad.days: Not published.
abroad.opening: not published as a non-resident product. The convention restates that a person 'de nationalité française résidant hors de France' who has no deposit account in France may ask the bank to open one with basic services, with refusals justified in writing and the Droit au Compte available. Opening normally requires an official photo ID, proof of address under 3 months old and a signature specimen.
abroad.kyc: At opening: an official photo ID, proof of address under 3 months old, a signature specimen and the self-certification of tax residence(s) and TIN(s). The client must keep information current, notably a change of tax residence, and provide a new self-certification when the country of tax residence changes, plus further documents on request. Failure can lead to refusal or closure at the bank's sole initiative. Forms by name (W-9 / W-8BEN) are not published.
abroad.taxAtSource: France: interest paid to a non-resident is exempt from French tax (CGI art. 125 A III) unless the person lives in an ETNC, where a 75% levy applies. No CSG/CRDS for non-residents (impots.gouv.fr).

SLATE assumes LBP charges no non-resident surcharge, since none is published, so the student pays the standard 2.10 EUR/month.
SLATE assumes the January 2025 convention is the one in force. Search results mention an October 2025 version that was not read.

de-deutsche-bank.conditions: No Deutsche Bank document read says the account ends when the customer moves abroad. Its address-change form (Auftrag zur Adressänderung, form code 250403) lets the customer give a foreign registered address and tick 'Steuerausländer (Ich habe in Deutschland weder einen Wohnsitz, auch keinen Nebenwohnsitz, noch meinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt)'. The same form says the account continues unchanged and that all agreed terms and conditions stay in force. The customer must report the new address and the change in tax residency. Product restriction: the price list says 'Das Junge Konto' (EUR 0.00 a month) is for pupils, apprentices and students up to age 30 'mit Meldeadresse im EU-Inland', and that once a condition lapses it 'wird ... als db AktivKonto weitergeführt' (EUR 6.90 a month). A student who moves to the US therefore keeps the account, but it becomes an AktivKonto. The bank may still end the account by ordinary notice: the Deutsche Bank BFSG payment-account information (1.11) says the bank must give at least two months' notice (AGB-Banken Nr. 19(1); BGB §675h(2)), and that there is no notice period for termination for cause.
de-deutsche-bank.nonResidentFee: No separate non-resident fee published. The standard model prices apply: db AktivKonto EUR 6.90 a month, db BestKonto EUR 13.90 a month. 'Das Junge Konto' (EUR 0.00) needs an EU registered address, so a US-resident student pays the AktivKonto price.
de-deutsche-bank.usResidentPolicy: Not published. Deutsche Bank does not say that it refuses or closes current accounts of US persons or US residents. Its FATCA/CRS self-certification (Selbstauskunft) asks about US citizenship, a green card and US birthplace, and requires an IRS Form W-9 from US citizens and US tax residents. It also says the bank may not open newly requested accounts without a valid tax self-certification (§3a(2) FKAustG).

abroad.card: Deutsche Bank Card (debit) used to pay in foreign currency outside the EEA ('sonstige Verfügungen'): 1%, minimum EUR 1.50. On top of that there is a currency-conversion fee: a 0.50% mark-up on the Mastercard/Visa rate (PLV ch. D 2.2.2). The Entgeltinformation AktivKonto (23.09.2026) also lists the debit card for payments in foreign currency at 1%, minimum EUR 1.50, charged on the card amount.
abroad.atm: Deutsche Bank Card at foreign ATMs in foreign currency: 1%, minimum EUR 5.99, plus the 0.50% currency-conversion mark-up, plus any fee the ATM operator sets. At the bank's foreign cooperation partners, which include Bank of America (USA), there is no Deutsche Bank fee, only the currency-conversion fee. The Entgeltinformation counts cash withdrawals in foreign currency at cooperation partners' ATMs as part of the account package.
abroad.outgoing: Transfers to non-EEA countries (Drittstaaten), all currencies, paperless/online, SHARE: 1.5 per mille of the amount, minimum EUR 10.00, plus EUR 1.55 Porto/SWIFT. OUR (sender pays all) adds a EUR 25.00 Fremdspesenpauschale. Urgent ('eilig') execution adds EUR 10.00 (PLV ch. B 2.2).
abroad.incoming: Incoming transfers charged under SHARE or BEN: EUR 5.50 up to EUR 2,500; EUR 10.00 from EUR 2,500 to EUR 12,500; 1 per mille above EUR 12,500, maximum EUR 95.00. These charges are deducted from the amount before it is credited (PLV ch. B 2.3). A SEPA credit in EUR is part of the account package.
abroad.fxMargin: Bank rate (DB-Abrechnungskurs) = WM/Reuters reference rate plus or minus a fixed mark-up per currency. For consumers the EUR/USD mark-up is 0.0050 USD per EUR (roughly 0.45% at 1.10). The rates are published on db-markets.com (PLV ch. D 1.2 b aa).
abroad.days: Non-EEA outgoing: 'Überweisungen werden baldmöglichst bewirkt'; no maximum is stated. Incoming: credited no more than one bank business day after the bank receives the funds.
abroad.opening: Not published for a US resident. The BFSG payment-account information gives a right to a Basiskonto only to people lawfully resident in the EU, people with no fixed address, asylum seekers and people with a Duldung, so a US resident has no Basiskonto right. Deutsche Bank's own account-opening and promotion terms require a main residence in Germany (seen only in a search-result snippet of its campaign Teilnahmebedingungen).
abroad.kyc: Tax self-certification under FATCA and CRS (FKAustG §3a): the customer states whether they are tax resident only in Germany, in Germany and abroad, or only abroad, and gives the foreign tax ID. A US citizen or US tax resident must provide an IRS Form W-9; a non-US person receiving US-source FDAP income must provide a W-8-series form. When moving, the customer uses the address-change form and declares Steuerinländer or Steuerausländer status. Under the BMF guidance, the bank stops withholding as for a resident only when it receives written proof of the move, such as the Abmeldung or a foreign tax-residence certificate. jp-mufg.conditions: MUFG publishes a dedicated non-resident service, 'Global Direct' (グローバルダイレクト), for customers who leave Japan 'with a plan to return' (帰国予定のあるお客さま) for one of: an overseas posting from a domestic employer, work at a Japanese embassy/consulate, STUDY AT A SCHOOL ABROAD (海外の学校への留学), or as accompanying family. It must be applied for in person at a branch at least 10 bank business days before departure (15 if Mitsubishi UFJ Direct is opened at the same time); 'customers who have already left Japan cannot newly apply' (出国済みのお客さまは、本サービスを新規にお申し込みいただくことはできません). Students must bring a certificate showing study period, school name and school address (e.g. admission letter, 入学許可証). Foreign nationals may apply but must also submit a residence card (在留カード), special permanent resident certificate, or a certified copy of the resident register. Customers moving to an OFAC-sanctioned country cannot apply. Once abroad, investment trusts, mortgage applications and some other transactions are unavailable to overseas residents; the address change for a move abroad (出国) must be done at a branch, not online, and is impossible online if the customer holds investment trusts, public bonds or general zaikei savings. The Japanese-national vs foreign-national distinction: under the Foreign Exchange Act a Japanese national becomes a non-resident on leaving to stay abroad 2+ years (or after 2 years abroad); a foreign national is presumed a non-resident unless working at an office in Japan or 6+ months after entry, so a foreign national who leaves Japan becomes a non-resident immediately. MUFG's ordinary deposit rules (普通預金規定, as of 2026-04-01) require non-Japanese depositors 'residing in Japan' to evidence a lawful status and period of stay and let the bank restrict withdrawals and other transactions once the notified period of stay has expired. Bank-initiated closure clause: the bank may suspend or close the account 'by notifying the depositor' for listed causes (illegal/AML/sanctions use, false KYC, organized-crime ties, inappropriate continuation); closure takes effect when the notice is dispatched to the registered name and address, 'regardless of whether it arrives' (到達のいかんにかかわらず…発信した時に解約). No notice period is stated. Accounts opened on/after 2021-07-01 that go 2+ years unused (and hold no other assets/loans) incur an 'unused-account management fee' of JPY 1,320/year, and if the fee cannot be debited the bank may close the account by notice.
jp-mufg.nonResidentFee: Global Direct: JPY 300/month (non-taxable), debited on the 18th of the following month from the Mitsubishi UFJ Direct representative yen account; JPY 330/month incl. consumption tax for customers who remain Foreign-Exchange-Act residents (e.g. embassy staff). Separately, the unused-account management fee of JPY 1,320/year applies to accounts opened from 2021-07-01 that are unused for 2+ years and hold no other assets.
jp-mufg.usResidentPolicy: MUFG publishes a FATCA page: when opening an account 'or when moving to the United States' (米国への転居をされる際など) it may ask for documents to establish whether the customer is a US taxpayer ('US person etc.': US citizens, anyone born in the US, green-card holders, and anyone residing in the US, with the substantial-presence day test spelled out: 31+ days this year and 183+ days weighted over 3 years). US persons' name, address, account number, TIN, balance and interest are reported to the IRS with the customer's consent (情報開示に関する同意書). If the customer does not cooperate with the FATCA check, a new account cannot be opened, but 'customers who already hold an account may keep it as it is' (口座をそのままお持ちいただけます), though account information may be passed to the IRS via the National Tax Agency on treaty-based request. Nothing published says MUFG closes accounts of US residents or US persons.

abroad.card: Mitsubishi UFJ-VISA Debit: Visa's reference rate + 3.05% (海外事務手数料). JCB debit: JCB reference rate + 3.05% + 1.6% JCB-designated rate (FAQ 619, 2019-10-01). Whether a non-resident may keep the debit card is not published.
abroad.atm: Debit card at overseas ATMs: JPY 110 per withdrawal (incl. tax) + the same 3.05% foreign transaction margin (Visa) + any fee set by the ATM operator. The ordinary cash card does not work at overseas ATMs (not separately confirmed for MUFG; SLATE assumption).
abroad.outgoing: Overseas remittance via Mitsubishi UFJ Direct (internet banking): JPY 2,500 to an MUFG overseas branch/local subsidiary, JPY 3,000 to another bank (e.g. a US bank). Branch counter / 'Foreign Remittance Web Support+': JPY 7,000 (+JPY 500 for a handwritten form). Plus, when sending in yen (円建), a yen-exchange handling fee of 0.05% (min JPY 2,500), or for same-currency sends from a foreign-currency deposit 0.05% x TTS (min JPY 2,500). Direct transfers are 'beneficiary pays' only; for 'remitter pays' at the counter, a paying-bank fee of JPY 3,000 is added. Non-residents' domestic yen transfers are themselves treated as foreign remittances: JPY 800 (to MUFG) / JPY 900 (other banks).
abroad.incoming: Receiving from abroad, foreign currency credited to a yen account: handling fee (被仕向送金取扱手数料) JPY 1,500 (if the amount is under JPY 3,000, half the amount); foreign currency into a same-currency foreign-currency account: free; yen into a yen account: JPY 1,500 handling + yen-exchange fee 0.05% (min JPY 2,500) for amounts JPY 8,000+. Fees paid by beneficiary unless the sender's bank pays. MUFG has announced revisions to part of the incoming fees from 2026-10-01 and 2026-12-14 (notice of 2026-03-02); the published notice appears to touch corporate fees and small amounts and keeps the free categories free for individuals.
abroad.fxMargin: Outgoing in foreign currency from a yen account uses MUFG's published TTS rate on the remittance date; incoming foreign currency converted to yen at the TTB rate on the credit date. The spread over mid-rate is not stated on the fee page (not fetched from the rate page).
abroad.days: Counter remittances take about 3 business days to execute (official). Online: not published.
abroad.opening: Not possible for the services that matter: Global Direct cannot be newly applied for after departure (official). MUFG's ordinary account opening requires Japanese identity documents and, for foreign nationals, residence-status evidence; nothing published offers account opening to a person already living abroad. MUFG does publish the reverse: an account-introduction service to U.S. Bank for MUFG customers in Japan (18+, holding a US visa, moving to the US within about 90 days), applied for by mail before departure.
abroad.kyc: Under Japan's CRS law (実特法, from 2017-01-01) customers must declare their country of tax residence, and must file a change notice (異動届出書) 'by the day 3 months after' the residence country changes; MUFG reports specified non-residents' accounts to the tax office by 30 April each year for automatic exchange. Global Direct application requires passport (photo and filled-in holder page), My Number documents, and for students the school's certificate of study period/name/address. FATCA: a customer moving to the US may be asked to establish US-person status and, if a US person (citizen, green card, or substantial-presence US resident), to sign a disclosure consent; the bank's FATCA page does not name the US forms (W-9/W-8BEN) by number. Non-Japanese depositors must keep their residence status/period of stay updated; unanswered confirmation requests by the set deadline let the bank restrict withdrawals.
abroad.taxAtSource: 15.315% national (income tax + reconstruction surtax) on deposit interest paid to a non-resident; Global Direct page: on leaving Japan the bank stops withholding local tax (5% 利子割) and resumes it on return. US-Japan treaty as amended by the 2013 protocol (in force 2019-08-30): interest is in principle exempt at source, applicable to amounts payable from 2019-11-01, if a treaty claim (租税条約に関する届出書) is filed via the payer before payment. Whether MUFG accepts such a claim for ordinary deposit interest is not published.

assumptions: SLATE assumes a Japanese-national Yale student who leaves Japan for a 4-year degree (so a Foreign-Exchange-Act non-resident) and applies for Global Direct before departure keeps the account at JPY 300/month; one who leaves without applying keeps a domestic-terms account only until the bank learns of the overseas address, after which online international transfers are unavailable and the bank may restrict the account.

SLATE assumes a foreign national who lived in Japan and leaves to study can keep the account only through Global Direct (which MUFG opens to foreign nationals with a residence card and a return plan); without it, once the registered period of stay expires the bank may restrict withdrawals and other transactions under the deposit rules, which in practice means the account should be closed before leaving.
SLATE assumes the ordinary MUFG cash card cannot be used at US ATMs (MUFG publishes overseas ATM use only for the debit card).
SLATE assumes a bank-initiated closure under the deposit rules can happen with no notice period (effective on dispatch), so closesWithNoticeDays is left null rather than 0.
SLATE assumes MUFG withholds 15.315% on a non-resident's deposit interest unless a treaty form is accepted; nothing published says MUFG processes treaty claims for deposit interest.

jp-japan-post-bank.conditions: Japan Post Bank (ゆうちょ銀行) FAQ 819 (published 2020-03-04): because it has no way to send notices abroad, it asks customers going on a long overseas posting to close their accounts 'as far as possible' (可能な限り…解約); if there is a continuing purpose such as salary deposits, the account may be kept after filing a non-resident notification (非居住者の届け). Non-residents' domestic transfers are treated as a special category (since 2022-05-06): JPY 7,500 at direct branches/eligible post offices, JPY 3,000 via app/Madotab/Yucho Direct, not available at ATMs; scheduled transfers not allowed. Foreign Exchange Act definitions used by the bank: Japanese nationals become non-residents if staying abroad 2+ years, working at a foreign office, or after 2 years abroad; foreign nationals are non-residents if in Japan under 6 months without domestic employment. Foreign nationals: Japan Post Bank's common deposit rules (version 202610) require non-Japanese residents to show proof of their period of stay, and new deposits are allowed only if the person will stay in Japan more than 3 months; its rules also let it restrict transactions once the notified period of stay is exceeded (search snippet). Overseas residents cannot open new accounts (FAQ 1147, snippet). Bank-closure clause notice period: not extracted (PDF text unreadable); a snippet of the rules mentions restrictions taking effect when a notice arrives or 1 month after dispatch, but which clause that is was not confirmed.

kr-kb-kookmin.conditions: Nothing KB publishes closes an account because the holder moves abroad to study. KB's security-centre pages assume customers keep using internet and mobile banking abroad. They say to cancel the overseas-IP-block service before leaving. ARS authentication does not work abroad, but an 'overseas departure confirmation' (해외출국사실 확인) button checks the Ministry of Justice immigration record and lets transfers proceed without ARS. KB also runs a '월드종합서비스' for overseas Koreans, covering remittances, FX, domestic transfers and deposit maturity after departure (reported in the press, not read on a KB page). Conditions in practice: keep a Korean phone in the holder's own name for phone verification (a foreign or prepaid USIM 'makes it difficult', per the KB FAQ), keep the CDD/KYC refresh current, and notify changes of address and phone (standard deposit terms, art. 14). Under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act a Korean national abroad for 2 years or more counts as a non-resident (Enforcement Decree art. 10(2)(5)(da)). That changes which FX services are open: KB's foreign-currency passbook excludes non-residents, for example. It does not end the KRW account. A KRW account untouched for 5 years becomes dormant (휴면예금): the contract ends automatically and the balance can be transferred to the Korea Inclusive Finance Agency (standard terms art. 9-2, as published by Hana, a standard industry clause).

kr-kb-kookmin.usResidentPolicy: Nothing published about refusing or closing accounts of US persons. Under the Korea-US FATCA agreement, Korean banks identify US-person accounts and report them to the NTS, which passes them to the IRS (FSC release).

A search snippet of KB's own fee page (obank C104041) gave internet-banking remittance fees of KRW 3,000 (≤US$5,000) / KRW 5,000 (>US$5,000). The page itself could not be fetched. Students: a 유학생송금 (overseas-student remittance) route exists and needs a designated FX bank (거래외국환은행 지정).
abroad.incoming: Foreign-currency incoming remittance: KRW 10,000 per transfer (KBthink article 2026-01-09); a search snippet of KB's fee page says it is waived under US$100 equivalent
abroad.fxMargin: KB's posted telegraphic-transfer rate (전신환매도율) with a preferential discount by channel/product (e.g. 30% on Quick Send). The margin itself is not published as a percentage.
abroad.days: Quick Send: up to one business day; standard SWIFT: not published on pages read
abroad.opening: Not possible remotely for a non-resident, per what was found. KB's non-face-to-face opening needs phone verification through a Korean carrier in the applicant's own name; with a foreign carrier or prepaid USIM, opening 'becomes difficult' (KB FAQ, via a search snippet). KB's foreigner pages cover registered foreign residents in Korea only.
abroad.kyc: Customer due diligence under the Act on Reporting and Using Specified Financial Transaction Information art. 5-2: identity, purpose of transactions and source of funds. It is re-done periodically, and a customer who refuses has existing business terminated. The refresh interval is not published by KB; a vendor source says 1-3 years. The standard terms require changes of address and phone to be notified (art. 14). FATCA/CRS: banks identify US persons under the Korea-US IGA. The Korean form is a residence-country self-certification (거주지국 신고서); a W-9 for a US person is not named on any KB page read. For the 유학생송금 route the bank requires a passport and an admission letter, then each year proof of enrolment, a tuition receipt and the previous semester's grades (per Hana's FAQ, a regulation-driven requirement).
abroad.taxAtSource: See countries.KR: domestic 20% income tax plus 10% local income tax (22% total) on non-resident interest; Korea-US treaty caps interest at 12%. Residents: 14% + 1.4% = 15.4%.

assumptions: SLATE assumes KB's general deposit terms match the industry-standard 예금거래기본약관 read in Hana's published copy. That copy has no fixed notice period for bank-initiated closure: an important declaration such as termination must be in writing and takes effect on arrival (art. 16(3)), and term changes are notified 1 month ahead (art. 21).

SLATE assumes a student who keeps a Korean phone number (e.g. roaming or a number-keeping plan) keeps full app access, and one who drops it loses phone-verification-dependent functions.

au-commbank.conditions: No published rule requires closure on moving abroad. CBA's T&Cs (TSIA, 1 Oct 2026) say: 'If you're a non-resident, we may be required to withhold a portion of your interest earned on the account.' The 'Confirm your details' page requires current residential address and tax residency. 'If you don't update your personal details, we may need to restrict access to your account/s until you do. We'll let you know about this at least 30 days before any account restrictions would apply.' Foreign tax residency is updated in NetBank under My Details > Citizenship, Residency and Tax Residency, or with an Individual Tax Residency Self-Certification Form. CBA publishes no separate non-resident account type for existing customers, and no 'moving overseas' page. Bank closure falls under TSIA clause 5.4: 'We may close your account after giving you reasonable notice.' No number of days is given. Under clause 5.4 CBA may also close the account without notice in listed circumstances, for example a balance under $10 unused for 3 months.

No published refusal or closure of accounts held by US persons or US residents.

abroad.card: 3.5% of transaction value for purchases made overseas, or in Australia with an overseas merchant/processor (TSIA fee table 3.2, 1 Oct 2026)

abroad.outgoing: Transfer fee waived for IMTs in NetBank or the CommBank app where the payment is converted to foreign currency (e.g. AUD to USD to a US account). $30.00 for AUD-to-AUD IMTs (no FX conversion) and for branch transfers. abroad.fxMargin: Not published as a percentage. Customers 'lock in the exchange rate' that CBA quotes in NetBank or the app when converting.
abroad.days: 'IMT's usually take 1 business day to be delivered, but can take longer depending on the overseas country, correspondent and recipient bank requirements'
abroad.opening: Only for people migrating to Australia. The migrant Everyday Smart Access account can be opened 'up to 14 days before you arrive' or within 12 months after arriving. Visitor visas (subclasses 600, 601, 651) are not accepted. ID must be shown at an Australian CBA branch within 20 days or the account closes automatically. No published route for a non-resident who is not moving to Australia.
abroad.kyc: CBA asks customers to confirm their full name, residential address, date of birth, occupation and tax residency, and restricts the account if they don't (at least 30 days' notice). CRS self-certification (Individual Tax Residency Self-Certification Form) with a foreign TIN, or reason code A/B/C if there is none. US citizens and US tax residents must give their US TIN. SLATE assumes CBA's exchange-rate margin is not modelled as a number, because CBA publishes no percentage.

nz-bnz.conditions: BNZ's Standard Terms and Conditions (1 Oct 2026) provide for non-residents. Clause 4.10: 'If you are a non-resident and ask us to, we can, at our discretion, elect to pay Approved Issuer Levy ... instead of deducting Non-Resident Withholding Tax'. Clause 4.11: 'You should tell us as soon as you can of any change in your tax rate or your tax residence status.' Clause 2.9 requires notice of changes to residential address and contact details. BNZ's app-setup support covers customers who 'reside overseas'. Clause 8.2 lets BNZ close or suspend an account 'for any reason'. Clause 8.3: 'We will not usually close your account ... unless we have told you that we are going to do so at least 14 days in advance.'

abroad.kyc: Clause 2.9: tell BNZ of changes to residential address and other details. Clause 4.11: tell BNZ of a change in tax residence. Clause 11.3: provide any information needed for NZ or overseas law. Tax-residency self-certification applies under FATCA/CRS. No W-9/W-8BEN is published. Without an IRD number, RWT is deducted at the 45% non-declaration rate (clause 4.9), which is relevant only while resident.

US.nonResidentWithholding: 0% on bank deposit interest paid to nonresident aliens when it is not effectively connected with a US trade or business (IRC 871(h) and 871(i)(2)(A); IRS 'Nontaxable types of interest income for nonresident aliens', reviewed 16-Sep-2026). A valid Form W-8BEN is needed. Without one, a bank may apply 24% backup withholding or 30% chapter 3 withholding. Deposit interest of $10 or more paid to an NRA resident in a country listed in Rev. Proc. 2024-42 is reported on Form 1042-S (income code 29, chapter 3 exemption code 02), so the IRS can exchange it with that country. The statutory rate on other US-source FDAP income of foreign persons is 30% (Pub. 515, 2026).

CA.nonResidentWithholding: 0% on ordinary bank-deposit interest paid at arm's length. The CRA says: 'Generally, the interest that you receive or that is credited to you is exempt from Canadian withholding tax if the payer is unrelated (arm's length) to you' (Non-residents of Canada page, modified 2026-01-20). ITA s.212(1)(b), current to 2026-09-21, imposes the 25% Part XIII tax only on interest that is not fully exempt and is paid to a non-arm's-length person, or on participating debt interest. A Canadian bank paying deposit interest to an unrelated customer is at arm's length.

MX.nonResidentWithholding: LISR art. 166 fracc. II inciso a): 4.9% withholding on interest paid to residents abroad on 'préstamos u otros créditos a cargo de instituciones de crédito' (a bank deposit is a credit against the bank). US-Mexico income tax convention (1992) art. 11(2): (a) 4.9% on interest from loans granted by banks/insurers or traded bonds; (b) 10% where the beneficial owner is not a person in (a) and the interest is 'paid by banks, including investment banks and savings banks'; (c) 15% otherwise. For a US-resident individual receiving deposit interest from a Mexican bank the treaty cap is 10%, so the domestic 4.9% applies (the lower rate). A US citizen/green-card holder remains taxable in the US on the interest regardless.

GB.nonResidentWithholding: None at source on UK bank/building society deposit interest. From 6 April 2016 'the obligation on banks and building societies to deduct tax at source from payments of interest on accounts was removed' (HMRC, Deduction of Income Tax from savings income). GOV.UK: 'Income Tax is no longer automatically taken from interest on savings and investments.' For a person non-resident for the whole tax year, ITA 2007 s.811 caps the UK liability on 'disregarded income' (which includes bank interest) at the tax deducted at source. Since nothing is deducted, the UK liability on the interest is in practice nil, though the person loses the personal allowance (HMRC SAIM1170). GOV.UK also says double-taxation-agreement relief can be claimed.

IE.nonResidentWithholding: DIRT at 33% (rate for 2020 onward, still in force in 2026) is deducted from deposit interest by Irish financial institutions. It is not charged on interest to individuals who are not resident in Ireland, have completed a non-resident declaration (a written form prescribed by Revenue and supplied by the bank), do not pay tax in Ireland, and have no joint account with an Irish resident. All beneficial owners must be non-resident. If DIRT is deducted, a non-resident in a treaty country (the US has a treaty with Ireland) can claim a refund on Form IC5.

IS.nonResidentWithholding: Interest paid by Icelandic payers to an individual resident abroad is taxable in Iceland. It is withheld at 12% where no double taxation treaty applies, and the withholding is final (no Icelandic return needed if this is the only Icelandic income). The Iceland–US treaty gives full exemption from Icelandic tax on interest (as do Denmark, Norway, the Faroes, Sweden, Finland and the UK). The exemption is requested in advance on form RSK 5.42, generally before the end of the tax year, or tax withheld is refunded on RSK 5.43. The domestic capital income tax (fjármagnstekjuskattur) rate is 22%. Source: Skatturinn guidance published on island.is ('Skattar af fjármagnstekjum einstaklinga sem búsettir eru erlendis').

DE.nonResidentWithholding: None on ordinary bank-deposit interest paid to a non-resident with no German residence or habitual abode. Limited German tax liability on interest under §49(1) Nr. 5 c EStG covers §20(1) Nr. 5 and 7 income only where the capital is secured by German real property or ships, or consists of certain profit-participation rights. Nr. 5 d covers over-the-counter coupon business (Tafelgeschäfte). Plain deposit interest is therefore not German-source income for a non-resident. BMF 14.05.2025 'Einzelfragen zur Abgeltungsteuer', Rn. 313: where no limited tax liability arises, the paying agent withholds no Kapitalertragsteuer. The bank must know the customer is non-resident. Rn. 314: when a customer reports a move abroad, the bank may stop assuming unlimited tax liability only on written, conclusive proof, such as the registration-office record of the move (Abmeldung) or a residence certificate from the foreign tax authority. Without proof it keeps treating the customer as resident and withholds 25% Abgeltungsteuer plus 5.5% Solidaritätszuschlag (26.375%) and church tax if applicable, less any Freistellungsauftrag. A Freistellungsauftrag ceases to be valid once unlimited tax liability ends. Note: an F-1 student who keeps a German Wohnsitz, for example a registered flat, can remain unlimitedly taxable in Germany, and then the 26.375% applies.

ES.nonResidentWithholding: General IRNR rate on interest without a permanent establishment: 19% (AEAT, tipos de gravamen IRNR; LIRNR art. 25). Exempt: (a) 'los rendimientos de las cuentas de no residentes' unless paid to a permanent establishment in Spain (LIRNR, RDLeg 5/2004, art. 14.1.d), so in practice 0% on a Spanish account properly flagged as non-resident; (b) interest to residents of other EU states, and from 2021-01-01 EEA states with effective tax-information exchange (art. 14.1.c). For a US resident: the Spain-US treaty as amended by the 2013 Protocol (published in the BOE 2019-10-23, in force 2019-11-27) generally removed source-state tax on interest (taxable only in the state of residence, with an anti-abuse rule for contingent interest), so the treaty also gives 0%. NOTE: the brief suggested art. 14 as the exemption for non-resident accounts; it is letter d (letter c is the EU/EEA exemption), checked on the BOE consolidated text (last updated 2023-05-25 per the page).

JP.nonResidentWithholding: Deposit interest (預貯金の利子, 'interest etc.') paid to a non-resident: 15.315% withheld (income tax 15% + reconstruction special income tax), NTA Tax Answer No.2884 (law as of 2026-04-01); from 2027 the components become income tax + defense special income tax + reconstruction special income tax (SLATE assumes the 15.315% total is unchanged; the NTA page lists only the current rate). Residents pay 20.315% (15.315% national + 5% local 利子割), NTA No.1310; the 5% local tax is not withheld from non-residents (MUFG Global Direct and SMBC Global Service both state local tax stops on departure). US-Japan treaty: under the 2013 protocol (in force 2019-08-30, applying to withholding on amounts payable from 2019-11-01) interest is in principle exempt in the source country (previously 10%, with financial institutions exempt), except profit-linked interest (10%) and above-arm's-length interest (5%); relief requires a 'Notice concerning a tax treaty' (租税条約に関する届出書) filed through the payer before the payment date, and when a treaty rate applies the surtax is not added.

KR.nonResidentWithholding: Domestic law: interest paid to a non-resident without a Korean PE is withheld at 20% income tax plus 10% local income tax, 22% in total. Interest on bonds issued by the State, local governments or domestic corporations is 14% + 1.4% = 15.4% (MOEF English publication, via search snippet; the securities-industry source says the same: 20% + 2%). Korea-US income tax treaty: interest capped at 12% (PwC worldwide tax summaries, reviewed 2026-06-04, official: false). PwC notes local income tax applies on top of the treaty rate generally; whether the Korea-US treaty's 12% already covers the inhabitant/local tax was not verified on an NTS page. Residents: 14% + 1.4% local = 15.4% on deposit interest; this standard figure was not re-read on an NTS page in this pass. To claim the treaty rate, the beneficial owner files a residency/beneficial-owner application with the withholding agent; the NTS publishes the forms.

AU.nonResidentWithholding: 10% of gross interest, a final tax, on interest paid by Australian banks to foreign residents (ATO: 'If you've given the financial institution your overseas address, the tax will be withheld at the rate of 10%'). If the bank lacks the overseas address and TFN, it may withhold at the top rate (47%). Foreign residents do not declare this interest in an Australian return. The ATO withholding-rate page notes the 10% applies unless a tax treaty specifies a lower rate.

NZ.nonResidentWithholding: NRWT on NZ-sourced interest: 15% standard, usually 10% for residents of double-tax-agreement countries (the US is one). Alternatively, a borrower registered as an approved issuer may pay Approved Issuer Levy of 2% of the interest instead of deducting NRWT. IRD lists 'New Zealand bank accounts of non-residents' among the securities that can be registered. In practice ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Westpac NZ and Kiwibank all deduct NRWT at the treaty/non-treaty rate by default and apply 2% AIL only on the non-resident's election or request, and BNZ and ANZ say at the bank's discretion or by agreement. The disadvantage of AIL is that it may not be creditable against tax in the country of residence (Westpac NZ).

us.foreignInterestForF1: An F-1 student who 'substantially complies with the requirements of the visa' is an exempt individual: their days in the US do not count toward the substantial presence test. They lose that status after being exempt as a teacher, trainee or student 'for any part of more than 5 calendar years', unless they show they do not intend to reside permanently. While exempt, the student is a nonresident alien. Nonresident aliens are 'taxed only on their income from sources within the United States and on certain income connected with the conduct of a trade or business in the United States' (Pub. 519). Interest is US-source only when paid by a US resident or domestic corporation, so interest from a home-country bank is foreign-source and not US-taxed. US bank deposit interest is also exempt under IRC 871(i)(2)(A). The student must still file Form 8843 for each year they exclude days, attached to Form 1040-NR or mailed alone if no return is required. Once the 5-calendar-year exemption ends and the student meets the substantial presence test, they become a resident alien taxed on worldwide income. From then the home-country interest is US-taxable and FBAR/Form 8938 can apply.
us.usPersons: US citizens and green-card holders (lawful permanent residents, under the green card test) are taxed on worldwide income, including interest from a foreign bank account (Pub. 519: resident aliens are 'generally taxed on their worldwide income, the same as U.S. citizens'). Foreign interest goes on Schedule B. Schedule B Part III, line 7a, asks whether at any time in the year the taxpayer had 'a financial interest in or signature authority over a financial account ... located in a foreign country'. The instructions say to answer 'Yes' even if FinCEN Form 114 is not required. A foreign tax credit (Form 1116) may offset any foreign withholding; SLATE did not research it further.
us.fbar: FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR): 'A United States person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file an FBAR if the aggregate value of the foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during the calendar year' (FinCEN). A US person means citizens, residents and US entities. Residency is decided by the IRC 7701(b) tests (green card test and substantial presence test) without regard to 6013(g)/(h) elections, and tax-treaty tie-breakers do not change it (IRS FBAR Practice Unit; 31 CFR 1010.350(b)). An F-1 student who is an exempt individual is therefore a nonresident alien and not a US person for FBAR. A US citizen or green-card holder is. The FBAR is due April 15 with an automatic extension to October 15. It is filed electronically through FinCEN's BSA E-Filing System, not with the tax return. Records must be kept for 5 years.
us.form8938: Form 8938 (FATCA, Statement of Specified Foreign Financial Assets) is filed by 'specified individuals': US citizens, resident aliens for any part of the year, and certain nonresident aliens (those electing to file jointly as residents, or bona fide residents of American Samoa or Puerto Rico). An F-1 nonresident alien is not one. Thresholds for an unmarried taxpayer living in the US: more than $50,000 on the last day of the tax year or more than $75,000 at any time during the year. Married filing jointly in the US: more than $100,000 or $150,000. Taxpayers living abroad have higher thresholds ($200,000/$300,000 single; $400,000/$600,000 joint). 'If you do not have to file an income tax return for the tax year, you do not need to file Form 8938.' Form 8938 does not replace the FBAR; both may be required.
us.fatca: Under FATCA, foreign financial institutions identify and report accounts of US persons. Treasury's FATCA page lists 114 jurisdictions with intergovernmental agreements, either in force or treated as in effect (e.g. Australia and Canada Model 1, 6-30-2014; Switzerland Model 2, 6-2-2014; Argentina Model 1, 1-1-2023; Thailand Model 1, 4-29-2024; China is listed as 'agreement in substance', Model 1). Russia is not on the list. Under a Model 1 IGA, banks report US accounts to their own tax authority, which passes the data to the IRS. Under a Model 2 IGA, banks register with the IRS and report directly with the account holder's consent. Foreign banks therefore ask customers for a US-indicia self-certification (W-9 for a US person) and report US persons' accounts. GAO-19-180 found that 'FFIs closed some U.S. persons' existing accounts or denied them opportunities to open new accounts after FATCA was enacted due to increased costs'. For an F-1 nonresident alien who is not a US citizen or green-card holder, FATCA does not make their home account reportable to the IRS. The home bank may still report it to the US-residence country under CRS once the student declares US tax residence, but the US does not take part in CRS.

assumptions: SLATE assumes that a resident current account held in any of the ~230 other countries and territories is kept on a conditional basis after its holder moves to the US to study. The bank may keep it, convert it to a non-resident account, restrict it, or close it under its general closure clause. Birthplace or citizenship alone grants nothing.

SLATE assumes that in the EU/EEA a bank may end a resident basic account when the holder is no longer legally resident in the Union (Payment Accounts Directive 2014/92/EU, Art. 19(2)(d)) with at least two months' written notice (Art. 19(4)). Under PSD2 (Directive 2015/2366, Art. 55(3)) a bank may end an open-ended payment-account contract with at least two months' notice if the contract allows it. SLATE uses 60 days as the EU/EEA notice default and has no default for countries outside the EU/EEA.

SLATE assumes that a holder who becomes a US person (US citizen, green-card holder, or a resident alien after the F-1 five-calendar-year exemption ends) is reported to the IRS by a foreign bank in any of the 114 jurisdictions on Treasury's FATCA IGA list. It also assumes some banks in those jurisdictions refuse or close accounts of US persons, as GAO-19-180 documented, and models this as a non-zero closure risk rather than a rule.

SLATE assumes that an F-1 nonresident alien who is not a US citizen or green-card holder is not a US person, so FATCA does not make their home account reportable to the IRS. The home bank may still ask for a CRS self-certification of the new tax residence. The US does not take part in CRS, so a declared US tax residence produces no CRS exchange to the US.

SLATE assumes that, where a country's banks charge non-residents a monthly account fee, the amount is not published in a form SLATE can verify for the ~230 countries. Non-resident fee is 'not published' and set to null by default, never invented.

SLATE assumes that an outgoing SWIFT transfer from a bank in any of these countries to a US account carries a sending-bank fee that SLATE has not researched country by country, plus possible correspondent and receiving-bank deductions and an FX margin. SLATE does not invent a per-country number. As a calibration only, the FSB's 2024 KPI report puts the global average cost of retail P2P cross-border payments at 2.6% and of a USD 200 remittance at 6.4% (USD 500: 4.3%), against G20 targets of 1% and 3%. Receiving US banks charge $0–$15 for an incoming international wire (Chase $15/$0, BofA $15, Wells Fargo $0, Citi $15, Capital One 360 none listed).

SLATE assumes that bank deposit interest paid to a non-resident is taxed at source at the country's domestic rate when no tax treaty applies, and at the treaty-reduced rate (the OECD Model Article 11(2) caps it at 10% of the gross interest) when a treaty with the US applies and the bank has the holder's residence certification. Many countries exempt bank deposit interest paid to non-residents entirely, as the US does under IRC 871(i)(2)(A). The domestic rate is not researched country by country for the ~230 countries and is 'not published' in SLATE until it is.

SLATE assumes that 131 jurisdictions on the OECD AEOI commitments list (last update 30 September 2026) exchange CRS account information. It also assumes the 42 developing countries listed as 'not asked to commit and that have not yet set a date' (e.g. Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Philippines, Viet Nam) do not exchange CRS data yet. This affects whether the home tax authority learns of a student's account abroad, not whether the home account is kept.

SLATE assumes that KYC refresh and a request for proof of address and a CRS/FATCA self-certification follow a change of residence everywhere. A holder who declares a US address or US tax residence must give a W-9 if a US person, or else a CRS self-certification naming the US as tax residence. A bank that cannot complete KYC on a non-resident may restrict or close the account under its general terms.
